newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: FOCUS - Issing - talk of softer EMU rules damaging.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Issing - talk of softer EMU rules damaging.

text.p: Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing on Thursday warned investor confidence in the planned European single currency was being undermined by recent talk of a possible softening of the entry criteria.

Issing said efforts by states to "window dress" their economic position to make the grade in 1997, the key year for judging which nations can join monetary union in 1999, were not helping to counter growing mistrust.

"Recently calls for a "political interpretation' -- the euphemism for a softening -- of the fiscal convergence criteria are likely to have further unsettled investors in their concern about the value of their savings," Issing said in a speech.
"Confidence in the stability of the future currency, the euro, is above all endangered by fears about a softening of the entry criteria."
The Bundesbank fully agreed with calls by the German parliament to interpret the criteria strictly and narrowly, Issing told a conference on monetary union in Luxembourg.
His comments were the latest in a Bundesbank campaign to ensure that the Euro will be stable and credible from the start.

The Bundesbank, one of the most powerful voices in the shaping of Europe's single currency, has attacked attempts by some countries to bend the rules as far as they can go to meet the entry requirements next year.

Under the terms of the Maastricht Treaty on European Union, countries seeking to qualify must meet strict goals on budget deficits, public borrowing, inflation and interest and exchange rates in 1997.

The Treaty states that a country's budget deficit must not exceed three percent of GDP and public debt must not be above 60 percent of GDP. But it allows for countries to qualify with higher levels under certain circumstances.
Issing said worries about the euro's stability were contributing to a reluctance to invest in shares and bonds.

This lack of money capital formation, which was also caused by uncertainty about the direction of interest rates, was hampering the slowdown in M3 money supply growth, the Bundesbank's main policy guide, Issing said.

He conceded the bank was likely to miss its 1996 goal for M3 of four-to-seven percent growth. But he said the trend towards a slowdown of M3 remained intact, despite a slight acceleration to 8.7 percent growth in August from 8.6 percent in July.

Issing also rejected recent calls by the Bank of England that countries outside EMU should have equal access to the planned payments system, known as Target, for the euro thereby, gaining access to intra-day credit in euros.
Reiterating the Bundesbank's opposition, Issing said equal access could hamper the future European central bank's ability to conduct monetary policy.
"Intraday credit can splash over into overnight credit and thereby, change central bank money supply and affect control of the money market," Issing said.
He denied that preventing EMU "outs" from equal access to Euro credit would be discriminatory.
